reviews.text: Saltburn, through its portrayal of Oliver, asks the middle class to look at themselves and what’s really driving their anti-rich sentiments.
reviews.author: Joseph Tomastik

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell’s second feature goes further than you’d think and finally twists the knife in your side, but you can’t help but be entertained.
reviews.author: Katie Hogan

reviews.text: It shares a propensity for treating its characters more as moveable, quippy pawns than as real people, a problem that the strong actors can only do so much to fix.
reviews.author: Christina Newland

reviews.text: Saltburn is a poignant satire of our society: from privilege to class struggle, the film highlights important issues we are more than familiar with today and points out the inherent contradictions within our world
reviews.author: Clotilde Chinnici

reviews.text: In fully utilizing its stylish flare and top-class performances, the film desperately attempts to mask the fact that it’s simply a rehash of class examination that never even manages to formulate an argument for its motives.
reviews.author: Yasmine Kandil

reviews.text: While its debaucherous presentation of lavish lifestyles may prove a bit much or strange for certain audiences, its strengths lie in its performances, assertive craftsmanship, and its critical, if perhaps somewhat muddy, themes on avarice.
reviews.author: Calum Cooper

reviews.text: A delicious sort of contradiction in Saltburn sets the tone for the entire film.
reviews.author: Stacey Yvonne

reviews.text: A carefully-constructed masterpiece...
reviews.author: Jessica Baxter

reviews.text: The film doesn’t really say anything new about the rich, or the social climbers who imitate them, but it’s plenty entertaining even as it veers into borderline camp territory in the final twenty minutes.
reviews.author: Sarah Marrs

reviews.text: Saltburn isn’t going to leave you feeling warm and fuzzy, but sometimes, I prefer to feel horrified and giggling to avoid my own discomfort. Buckle up for some fun.
reviews.author: Shadan Larki

reviews.text: Barry Keoghan steals the scenes. Keoghan plays a doe-eyed sociopath, obsessed, dark, and aloof, with such grounded insanity that it brings to mind his earlier roles in The Green Knight and The Killing of a Sacred Deer.
reviews.author: Jaylan Salah

reviews.text: It’s impossible not to sense the film completely slipping from her once the narrative begins unveiling a bold set of reveals in this final third.
reviews.author: Caleb Hammond

reviews.text: It’s Gothic stateliness by way of Goth subculture -- enter at your own risk.
reviews.author: Matt Brunson

reviews.text: These liaisons aren't nearly dangerous enough in Emerald Fennell's initially interesting but ultimately feckless exercise in the depravity of class issues and the polite homophobia of the mid-2000s.
reviews.author: Nicholas Bell

reviews.text:
Writer/director Emerald Fennell helps usher in 2023 as the year that Cinema vaulted back to life, with a transgressive black comedy that splashes cum-soaked mud on corporate cinema with tireless glee.

Comic book movies be damned.
reviews.author: Cole Smithey

reviews.text: You don’t get to feed us nonsense and then expect us to thank you when you try to explain it.
reviews.author: Fletcher Powell

reviews.text: Derivative it may be – the plot is a salad of ideas pinched from Evelyn Waugh, Patricia Highsmith and Pasolini – you won’t be bored for a second.
reviews.author: Jamie Dunn

reviews.text: It was impossible to shake the comparison to Ripley with Saltburn while I was watching it, but I still tried to revel in Fennell’s audaciousness, coupled with a truly game and committed performance from Keoghan.
reviews.author: Catherine Springer

reviews.text: Exasperatingly toxic psycho sexual drama - that varies between bizarre and disgusting
reviews.author: Susan Granger

reviews.text: A weird, intense movie that has the courage of its convictions.
reviews.author: Robert Levin

reviews.text: Barry Keoghan gives a brilliant performance as the complicated, many-sided Oliver Quick, ably supported by the rest of this talented cast. Writer-director Emerald Fennell creates a wicked study of social classes with some surprising plot twists.
reviews.author: Robert Roten

reviews.text: Saltburn sparked discussion, but for all its stylized images and clever gendered trope inversions, its queer promises are empty.
reviews.author: Evan Sawdey

reviews.text: A great time produced by a great director without being a great movie.
reviews.author: Chris Barsanti

reviews.text: Saltburn is a brilliant movie that is almost brought down by a poorly written ending.
reviews.author: Korey Coleman

reviews.text: Saltburn is pretty and plenty of its audience will delight in being able to say they were in on the joke whenever the film resurfaces on social media. A viral movie is not necessarily a good movie.
reviews.author: Ian Thomas Malone

reviews.text: A thing of grotesque beauty and sublime wit that is a testament to Ms. Fennell's talents as both a storyteller and a commentator on the absurdities of the human condition.
reviews.author: Andrea Chase

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell's definition of subtlety is bashing us over the head with a small Le Creuset frying pan rather than one of their massive casserole pots.
reviews.author: Sarah Cartland

reviews.text: Saltburn may be nihilistic and nasty, shallow and insubstantial, but in its own weird way, it's effective.
reviews.author: Alison Gillmor

reviews.text: Saltburn is a delicious cinematic schadenfreude.
reviews.author: Danielle Ryan

reviews.text: With audacious films like Visitor Q, it is possible to effectively weave salacious themes with substance. While Saltburn demands post film reaction, through shocking scenes or gorgeous shots, I grapple to find the emotional core of this film.
reviews.author: KT Mahe

reviews.text: Mesmerizes with its exploration of class and friendship, offering engaging storytelling over mere shock. It revises then reaffirms initial expectations, creating an intriguing yet somewhat unsatisfying inevitability.
reviews.author: Oti

reviews.text: Imagine the version of this written and directed by Boots Riley. Now think about why he doesn't get this sort of budget, yet Emerald Fennell does.
reviews.author: Walter Chaw

reviews.text: Much like Fennell's previous feature, Promising Young Woman, Saltburn shoots itself directly in the foot and renders its already-empty provocations that much more inert. What it then says about class is off-key at best and regressive at worst.
reviews.author: Chase Hutchinson

reviews.text: It piles on deviant provocations in the absence of originality or any insights into the English class system... But it is an irresistible watch, thanks to Keoghan’s shifty and sinister presence in the central role.
reviews.author: Whang Yee Ling

reviews.text: Saltburn knows it looks good. It’s just a shame it doesn’t know which story to tell.
reviews.author: Rosalynn Try-Hane

reviews.text: At first glance, Saltburn appears to be just another film about a young upstart trying to break into the insouciant, moneyed British aristocracy. But as the layers quickly begin peeling off, it becomes a compelling film that will haunt you.
reviews.author: Lisa Johnson Mandell

reviews.text: It’s best to take Promising Young Woman writer/director Emerald Fennell’s sophomore slump with a grain of salt. An underdeveloped homage to The Talented Mr. Ripley and Brideshead Revisited luxuriates in provocative fashion without substance.
reviews.author: Eric Marchen

reviews.text: This movie is for shock value. It is depraved, distasteful, disturbing. I don't know who is going to sit through this until the end. I am having little tolerance for movies that are weird just for weird sake.
reviews.author: Lynn Venhaus

reviews.text: Remember Dark Shadows or The Talented Mr. Ripley?  Emerald Fennell is giving us all that and more with her psychological thriller
reviews.author: Carla Renata

reviews.text: Saltburn is not quite the Hitchcockian psychological thriller the trailer built it up to be, but that doesn’t mean it’s not without its own merits. Saltburn is an ugly, shallow, and immaculate tale of obsession.
reviews.author: Tina Kakadelis

reviews.text: Saltburn”so regularly is a riot of its own distinct kind that it should keep many viewers entertained.
reviews.author: Mark Meszoros

reviews.text: A bit too predictable with characters I neither liked nor found joy in rooting against.
reviews.author: Kevin Carr

reviews.text: Fennell clearly with Promising Young Woman, & now this is a Writer/Director that people will pay attention to, yet for me, their endings still leave a lot to be desired & keep them from being a filmmaker I anticipate their subsequent work for right now.
reviews.author: Julian Lytle

reviews.text: Barry Keoghan dazzles in this sensual, enigmatic and twisted drama about class and power. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Rene Sanchez

reviews.text: The performances are acerbic... Pike's Elspeth is brilliantly cracked.
reviews.author: Mark Kermode

reviews.text: Director Fennell knows how to keep her story moving. It’s both wickedly funny and sharply serious and a terrific directorial juggling act. Just when you think everything is wrapped up, she delivers a surprise. A true jolt to your senses.
reviews.author: Michael Calleri

reviews.text: Far from Barry Keoghan's central performance and the visual style that often elegantly adorns the spaces of the mansion, on the surface it is nothing more than a somewhat banal black comedy about obsession, class and privilege. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Yasser Medina

reviews.text: Despite presenting an interesting satire, Satlburn suffers from clichés and lacks the necessary wit. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Juan Pablo Russo

reviews.text: This boundary-pushing, modern gothic thriller feels created to shock rather than to tell a fully realized story, and Fennell achieves a varying degree of success with her flawed (but memorable) sophomore effort.
reviews.author: Louisa Moore

reviews.text: This black comedy is smart, but mean – and ultimately hollow.
reviews.author: Tim Miller

reviews.text: While constantly daring, the film is uneven. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Randy Meeks

reviews.text: Posh against posh. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Rubén Romero Santos

reviews.text: Saltburn is not near as clever as it thinks and the shocking moments seem to only exist merely to get people talking. The awkward characters, witty dialogue, interesting setting and slick production; are more than enough to keep viewers engaged.
reviews.author: Adam Olinger

reviews.text: I am pulling no punches when I admit that Saltburn is one of my favorite movies of 2023. Emerald Fennell’s newest film is brave. It’s uncomfortable and it’s ready to make you revel in the weirdness.
reviews.author: Kimberly Pierce

reviews.text: Saltburn owes its lurid magnetism to the grotesque nature of the characters. We feel the hatred, lust and envy beneath Oliver’s deadpan demeanour, and the superficiality of Felix’s compassion, born from a life of shameless privilege.
reviews.author: John McDonald

reviews.text: Kudos go to Barry Keoghan, who gives his all as the sneakily manipulative Oliver Quick.
reviews.author: Casey Chong

reviews.text: Saltburn is made up of moments of supposed shock, clumsily linked to each other [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ricardo Gallegos

reviews.text: Fennell is trying to shock us, and maybe trying a little too hard. Not that we should complain too much -- the film is far from dull, just unfocused in its intent.
reviews.author: John Serba

reviews.text: This is a third date movie, where you’re comfortable watching other people put their genitals all over each other. Saltburn will spark uncomfortable silence. It may be a few days before you decide you love it. It’s been known to happen.
reviews.author: MontiLee Stormer

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell's provocative second feature comes dangerously close to demonising the downtrodden and feeling pity for the privileged, but, hey, at least it looks pretty.
reviews.author: Rohan Naahar

reviews.text: At first, 'Saltburn' seems like it wants to tell you an intriguing story about wealth, jealousy, sex, and misfortune. Yet, the result is an unconvincing protagonist floating in a sea of dull, rich people misbehaving.
reviews.author: Chauncey K. Robinson

reviews.text: Barry Keoghan, in one of the most fearless performances of the year, plays Oliver Quick, an enigmatic figure at Oxford who becomes obsessed with the gorgeous and filthy rich Felix (Jacob Elordi, filthy-handsome and terrific)...
reviews.author: Frank J. Avella

reviews.text: ... The film has undisputed suggestive and seductive power, but when that surface dissipates, the artifice, solemnity, and banality of a film with more aspirations than concrete findings are revealed. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Diego Batlle

reviews.text: The power of Barry Keoghan’s center-ring performance cannot be adequately over-praised.
reviews.author: Rex Reed

reviews.text: An expensively manufactured vase that writer-director Emerald Fennell forgot to fill.
reviews.author: Matt Pais

reviews.text: Barry Keoghan is the star of this film, and he damn well knows it...  well-acted, diabolical, and decadent, there’s an underlying sense of it being more of a dark fairy tale than anything taken too seriously.
reviews.author: Kevin A. Ranson

reviews.text: ...a watchable yet rather tedious sophomore effort from Fennell.
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: Entertaining but the movie seems to have been patched together from other familiar movies.
reviews.author: Jackie K. Cooper

reviews.text: Films about English class privilege used to be sane, continuing a proud tradition. Now the worst people in Hollywood make films about the worst people in the world. Fennell sells attitude to replace knowledge and feeling.
reviews.author: Armond White

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell's 'Saltburn' examines envy, classism and a murky romance in the shadow of a gothic-tinged mansion. But for all its ambition, the film falls short in how it tells its seemingly audacious story. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Aglaia Berlutti

reviews.text: The sexual groveling of Oliver is akin to the social groveling of anyone who worships the ultra rich simply for being rich.
reviews.author: Drew Gregory

reviews.text: Director Emerald Fennell continues to prove she is one of our most creative storytellers with Barry Keoghan, Rosamund Pike and Jacob Elordi giving standout performances.
reviews.author: Lauren Veneziani

reviews.text: Stupid careless rich people are always entertaining even if there's absolutely nothing new being said, and the numerous scenes here where class and status is undermined and then re-enforced have an engaging energy to them.
reviews.author: Anthony Morris

reviews.text: I admired SALTBURN's boldness, but as a dramatic and thematic exercise, it leaves a lot to be desired.
reviews.author: JD Duran

reviews.text: With excellent acting, arresting visuals and art direction to die for, this is one of the most original movies to be released in years.
reviews.author: Ben Turner

reviews.text: Possesses an originality re obsession that is deeper than the surface. Barry Keoghan's Oliver uplifts the emotions in his situations, and the supporting cast shines, especially Carey Mulligan and Rosamund Pike in key story moments. w/Emerald interview.
reviews.author: Patrick McDonald

reviews.text: Saltburn embraces that universally cosmic dread of being a revolting human being and builds an extravagant labyrinth of a castle on top of it. Saltburn is disgustingly mesmerizing, and Barry Keoghan gives the perverted performance of a lifetime.
reviews.author: Chris Sawin

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell’s latest provocation is tasty fare, if a bit unclear about who’s the main course.
reviews.author: Dorothy Woodend

reviews.text: Saltburn will get the town talkin’ that is for damn sure. Will this conversation stand the test of time? All signs point to: NO.
reviews.author: Rosalie Kicks

reviews.text: Consistently amusing—the film namechecks Evelyn Waugh, but the sardonic tone feels closer to Kingsley Amis—and the actors are a blast to watch interact with each other.
reviews.author: Sonny Bunch

reviews.text: The shock value here is quite....forward, but don't let that get in the way of the absolutely fierce performance by Barry Keogan.
reviews.author: Lee McCoy

reviews.text: Mr. Keoghan has an uncanny ability to come across as shifty and devious even in repose, and his performance is the key to the movie.
reviews.author: Kyle Smith

reviews.text: It is through its unapologetic manipulation that a movie which might easily otherwise have been just another mindless, lurid thriller [turn] into a savage piece of cinema that you’ll want to see again and again.
reviews.author: John Paul King

reviews.text: Unlike "Promising Young Woman," it doesn’t tap into the rage of its day. It’s just purposelessly unpleasant.
reviews.author: Rob Gonsalves

reviews.text: Fine, disreputable fun until what might be the stupidest, most misguided ending I’ve seen since… well, since Fennell’s previous picture.
reviews.author: Sean Burns

reviews.text: Fennell’s stunning visuals and Barry Keoghan’s excellence lift "Saltburn" to must-watch status.
reviews.author: Alan French

reviews.text: Disturbing and brilliant, with vile characters who will stay with you long after you make their acquaintance.
reviews.author: Linda Cook

reviews.text: This movie is a combination of Brideshead Revisited and The Talented Mr. Ripley. The first two acts are fantastic...but frankly the 3rd act goes off the rails with too many twists turns, trying to keep you engaged and it did not work for me.
reviews.author: Michael Cook

reviews.text: Fennell's filmmaking skills have vastly improved over the past three years, and her writing is even more ambitious.
reviews.author: Edwin Arnaudin

reviews.text: Saltburn isn't the same kind of movie as [Fennell's] debut, but it goes farther than you'd ever expect it to, and it definitely leaves you with the sense that you've seen something. Or, rather, that you've been punched in the eyes.
reviews.author: Jeffrey M. Anderson

reviews.text: A clever, queasy drama, with a terrific star turn from its lead actor, that dares to drive a twisted story about class envy and class war to a risky conclusion
reviews.author: Jane Freebury

reviews.text: We're asked to be shocked by developments that are, to be frank, predictable, and in the process, any pretense of meaningful class satire goes out the window.
reviews.author: Margot Harrison

reviews.text: Given the contempt and cynicism on display, the film is watchable enough; it certainly doesn’t hurt that most of the roles have been taken by beautiful people.
reviews.author: Robert W. Butler

reviews.text: Despite its shortcomings, Saltburn is transfixing both in its direction and its acting.
reviews.author: Kristian M. Lin

reviews.text: But by the end of it, I just felt like I I've seen this movie before.
reviews.author: Alonso Duralde

reviews.text: There’s fertile ground for satire here, but that would require a scalpel, and Fennell wields a blunt hatchet.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell’s deliciously dark comedy sticks the knife into the English class system and gives it a proper twist.
reviews.author: Philip De Semlyen

reviews.text:
Like “Promising Young Woman,” Fennell’s Oscar-winning film, “Saltburn” slices someone else’s life, then teaches us plenty about our own.

It’s a twisty, turny drama that will make you think twice about ever accepting another invitation.
reviews.author: Bruce R. Miller

reviews.text: [Keoghan] carries this diversionary tale of "eat the rich" politics right through a silly curtain lift that makes it seem Fennell thinks we're as vapidly dumb as the Cattons covering their eyes when THE RING is on TV.
reviews.author: Jared Mobarak

reviews.text: Love it or loathe it, Emerald Fennell’s deliciousl takedown of the upper classes keeps you glued to Barry Keoghan as a poorboy driven to madness and worse by a rich Adonis (Jacob Elordi) and his hilariously vampiric mom (an Oscar-ready Rosamund Pike).
reviews.author: Peter Travers

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell's Saltburn is diabolically entertaining.
reviews.author: M.N. Miller

reviews.text: It’s an entertaining film, but a mixed bag, filled with over-the-top moments and plot twists, but at the end it feels less than the sum of its parts.
reviews.author: Richard Crouse

reviews.text: A showcase for Keoghan with a bravura bare-all performance but all the boundary-pushing moments ultimately amount to a shallow and vile endeavor.
reviews.author: Ruth Maramis

reviews.text: The Talented Mr. Ripley for the cool kids.
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: Performances by Keoghan and Pike make this scenario work. It could have just worked a little better if Fennell had shown a little more courage in putting the twists into the finale.
reviews.author: Rick Bentley

reviews.text: In a short time, “Saltburn” has become one of the most divisive films of the year, and it's not hard to see why; I don't think Fennell's intentions were bad, but the final product certainly could have been better thought out. Full review in Spanish.
reviews.author: Sebastian Zavala Kahn

reviews.text: While I think the film is visually sumptuous and striking... It doesn't feel like it has a lot of substance.
reviews.author: Lael Loewenstein

reviews.text: It's good, but familiar.
reviews.author: Tim Cogshell

reviews.text: One expects this development will effectively end Oliver’s time at Saltburn, but it only serves to embolden Oliver and motivate him to show his true colors. Let’s just say Saltburn and many of its denizens will never be the same.
reviews.author: Richard Roeper

reviews.text: If reports of audiences clutching their collective pearls over male full-frontal nudity, masturbation, oral sex, baby-batter bathwater scandalizes you, then stay away from Yorgos Lanthimos’ films because they would devastate you.
reviews.author: Sarah Vincent

reviews.text: Fennell certainly has an eye for striking imagery, but has unfortunately yet to deploy it in a way that feels thematically coherent.
reviews.author: Mattie Lucas

reviews.text: Where Promising Young Woman was a revenge story, Saltburn is an entirely different beast--social power and class privilege will never be the same.
reviews.author: Danielle Solzman

reviews.text: The golden summer, the life-changing friendship, the fantasy location: they are all put under fantastical, acutely-realised pressure here. It’s an astonishing cinematic experience, both oddly light and viscerally nasty.
reviews.author: Keri O'Shea

reviews.text: Questionable late-movie choices don’t diminish Saltburn’s admirable qualities: its audacity, energy, and unpredictability.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell is a fearless director, Saltburn offers a cold-blooded but riotous ride through the minds of people who have spent too long looking into cracked mirrors hoping to see a reflection of something worthwhile looking back at them.
reviews.author: Nadine Whitney

reviews.text: Saltburn just goes too far, and its startling images shocked me out of the story altogether.
reviews.author: Alan Ng

reviews.text: Saltburn is a solid sophomore effort from Fennell and cements that she is one of the most talented filmmaking voices working today, but it is not as balanced as her debut film.
reviews.author: Alex Maidy

reviews.text: Fennell deserves praise for the way she continues to incorporate queer characters and storylines into her work. Where Saltburn goes slightly awry is that some scenes... feel endless.
reviews.author: Gregg Shapiro

reviews.text: The platonic romance between Oliver and Felix is just the icing on a somewhat bloated but undoubtedly lavish and tasty social satirical cake. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Gustavo Herrera Taboada

reviews.text: Certain to upset pious viewers while thrilling those who love twisted, decadent thrillers. And, oh my goodness, what an ending.
reviews.author: Randy Myers

reviews.text: Saltburn dazzles in its finale but stumbles through a disjointed narrative. Despite artistic strengths, uneven storytelling hinders its potential, falling short of Fennell's previous triumph in Promising Young Woman.
reviews.author: Jason Escamilla

reviews.text: Longing for someone can be a dangerous thing, and Emerald Fennell perfectly captures that in this imperfect queer masterpiece.
reviews.author: EJ Moreno

reviews.text: A character who acts without context or motivation is not compelling to me. Saltburn tries to shock us, again and again—instead, it ends up being a bit of an empty suit.
reviews.author: Max Weiss

reviews.text: There’s no one at all to like in Ms Fennell’s film, which may undermine its aspirations to moral seriousness. But it’s a bit of a laugh, especially early on.
reviews.author: Paul Whitington

reviews.text: “Saltburn” feels at times like a John Waters film as it moseys through “Talented Mr. Ripley” territory, occasionally taking a pit stop in Divine’s neck of the woods before reaching its Downton Abbey-on-poppers destination. Devilishly entertaining.
reviews.author: Joe Friar

reviews.text: Combining social satire and psychological thriller, “Saltburn” holds your attention, but its contrivances grow increasingly grating as it scrambles to its supposedly astonishing climax.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: Films set on ornate British estates tend to be stuffy period pieces, so Fennell’s story is initially a breath of fresh air, telling a more modern version that’s full of life.
reviews.author: Alex Bentley

reviews.text: Saltburn is neither biting nor smart, and its denouement lacks the mixture of joy, rage, and hopelessness many feel while stuck in the system’s fist.
reviews.author: Emily Wheeler

reviews.text: I've seen Keoghan in many movies but I barely recognized him in "Saltburn." It's a high-wire act and, even if "Saltburn" isn't always sure what it's doing, Keoghan never misses a beat.
reviews.author: Chris Hewitt

reviews.text: Visually, the movie can be quite pretty. Linus Sandgren, Damien Chazelle’s go-to cinematographer, shot it. Emotionally, it’s ugly through and through, which the prettiness makes that much uglier.
reviews.author: Mark Feeney

reviews.text: …slapdash, exhausting, vacuous…the kind of hambone justification of elite rule that couldn’t be more out of step with today…
reviews.author: Eddie Harrison

reviews.text: Saltburn toes the blurred line between a positive reclamation of the ‘evil gays’ trend and a negative stereotype.
reviews.author: Li Lai

reviews.text: The film has a good craft, the house they got for filming was stunning, but that is not enough for me to think something is a good movie.
reviews.author: Carson Timar

reviews.text: A risible and hollow Talented Mr. Ripley for the Euphoria generation.
reviews.author: Radheyan Simonpillai

reviews.text: Saltburn is neither a triumph nor catastrophe, which is often the case with directors making their sophomore efforts after exploding onto the scene. However, it is compelling enough to remain optimistic about one of Britain’s brightest filmmaking voices.
reviews.author: Victoria Luxford

reviews.text: 'Saltburn' continues the [Fennell's] grand ability to apply pressure. Not only can the characters feel that challenge with each other, but so can the audience with Fennell’s visuals and situational intensities. Inventive, bold and fearless!
reviews.author: Preston Barta

reviews.text: More formulaic and less genuinely audacious than it thinks it is, the film is an entertaining mix of dark comedy and psychological thriller, rich on morbid fun and intoxicating visuals. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Nestor Bentancor

reviews.text: While it’s whip smart and wickedly daring, “Saltburn” is also excessively repellant and depressing.
reviews.author: Russ Simmons

reviews.text: Saltburn is a summer-break journey into bourgeois excess and sociopathic tenacity that wrapped its seductive tentacles around my throat and then spent 127 glorious minutes gently tightening its slithery embrace.
reviews.author: Sara Michelle Fetters

reviews.text: Oliver Quick, portrayed by ever-reliably odd Barry Keoghan, (is) followed from a nice opening tracking shot entering Oxford, until a cleverly stunning closer of same almost saves writer/director Emerald Fennell's second real doozy of a film.
reviews.author: John Urbancich

reviews.text: Despite a mischievous audacity, it rarely digs beneath its surface provocations.
reviews.author: Todd Jorgenson

reviews.text: Sleek, smart, and in possession of a devious streak.
reviews.author: Mike McGranaghan

reviews.text: "Saltburn" might not be as original as the Oscar-winning "Promising Young Woman," but it promises its audience a wild ride and constant twists and turns that disgust and delight.
reviews.author: Matthew Creith

reviews.text: Saltburn -- by including images that invite averted eyes  -- can be viewed as a movie that dresses for dinner and then throws up on itself. On another, it's a daring comic display of the base motivations that underly class privilege.
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: Come for the class warfare and the occasional shots-fired zingers about the rich being different than you and me. Stay for Keoghan.
reviews.author: David Fear

reviews.text: Fennell loses her creative self within this glaringly phony world of debauchery and opulence. As a result, things like narrative structure, story progression, and character development get tossed aside for warped and edgier grasps for attention.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: A glossy romp through hipster affluence, Saltburn is all style and limited substance.
reviews.author: Morgan Rojas

reviews.text: It's a dark and twisted cross between Cruel Intentions and The Talented Mr. Ripley but super weird as sh**. I wanted to love this more but was mostly disappointed in the first 45 mins but the picks up in the 2nd half and ends on a strong note.
reviews.author: Elliott Collins

reviews.text: Fennell revels in excess and tries to comment on it, but none of it lands outside of the performances and lavish production value.
reviews.author: Andrew Parker

reviews.text: Saltburn comes across not primarily as a satire of the upper-class, but as a warning about the (too smart, too sexual, insufficiently heterosexual) rabble.
reviews.author: Noah Berlatsky

reviews.text: At times deliciously campy & twisted, and at others painfully simplistic & melodramatic, the story plays out much how you’ll expect, with provocation after provocation attempting to distract from the obvious lack of substance. But hey, it looks gorgeous!
reviews.author: Aaron White

reviews.text: Nothing about Saltburn is particularly surprising, although writer/director Emerald Fennell certainly seems to believe much of it is.
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: Keoghan convincingly embraces this complex young man and his conflicting emotions ... His portrayal is stellar and his utter commitment to the picture’s naked end is applaud-worthy.
reviews.author: Sarah Gopaul

reviews.text: This isn’t a deep psychological dive into normal versus psychopathy. Fennell is looking at the glossy surface of social climbing. Consequently, the film lacks the emotional bite that this kind of noir-ish satire demands.
reviews.author: Karen Gordon

reviews.text: Saltburn flails around a bit and sometimes feels confused, overwrought, overlong, even borderline campy. But stick with it. It ultimately adds up to a potent piece of moviemaking, and of storytelling.
reviews.author: M.V. Moorhead

reviews.text: Having put a high sheen on hoary narrative conventions, which prove seductive, “Saltburn” reveals itself as simply a pastiche of repackaged goods.
reviews.author: Charles Koplinski

reviews.text: This is an exquisitely shot, multilayered, psycho-sexual film that goes way too far. Fennell takes you on a shocking journey to find out who can master the game of riches in this salacious state of affairs that is Saltburn.
reviews.author: Linda and Al Lerner

reviews.text: How can a scholarship student at Oxford University relate to his privileged classmates? That’s the dilemma for poor Oliver Quick who looks as drab as others find him but has one advantageous attribute: he assesses individuals astutely
reviews.author: Diane Carson

reviews.text: Make no mistake, the clever writing is here, as is the style, the sleek technique, and some terrific performances (Rosamund Pike is especially delicious in a supporting role). What’s missing, or muddled, is the message -- and perhaps even more, the heart.
reviews.author: Jocelyn Noveck

reviews.text: Barry Keoghan brings the swagger in Emerald Fennell’s tasty black comedy.
reviews.author: Nate Adams

reviews.text: "Saltburn" is a revenge opera that's more silly than it is serious — "The Talented Mr. Ripley" for the millennial crowd — and it feels like one that Fennell needed to get out of her system in able to move forward.
reviews.author: Adam Graham

reviews.text: Keoghan delivers what can only be described as an impressively committed performance in a movie that, in the end, considers itself way more shocking than it really is.
reviews.author: Ann Hornaday

reviews.text: As a theatrical provocation, “Saltburn” is just what the doctor ordered.
reviews.author: Jonathan W. Hickman

reviews.text: There’s no depth to the images, no character who isn’t bent to the task of provocation, and nowhere for the story to go except a murderous spiral of jaw-dropping ludicrousness.
reviews.author: Tom Shone

reviews.text: Saltburn is a dizzying, wicked spell of lust, lies, and betrayal. It’s one of the best films I’ve seen all year, but I know it will be divisive for audiences.
reviews.author: Paul McGuire Grimes

reviews.text: Although the film takes place in this century, Fennell and her production team give it a timeless look, often with candlelight. It’s appropriate, as what’s unspooling is as old as human interaction.
reviews.author: Abbie Bernstein

reviews.text: Fennell has made a different kind of period film from The Talented Mr. Ripley and Brideshead Revisited. Saltburn is an indie sleaze fantasia for older millennials that succeeds more as a character study than a thriller.
reviews.author: Alan Zilberman

reviews.text: You can feel yourself getting fatter off its empty calories, but the dopamine hit is real, like eating a greasy-spoon cheeseburger after a night of heavy drinking. Or whatever the 1% equivalency might be.
reviews.author: Andrew Dignan

reviews.text: You watch wishing it were better, but nonetheless pulled into this dark story of a young man navigating a world where he’s invisible.
reviews.author: Moira MacDonald

reviews.text: If cameras have a caffeine-laced-with-acid filter, Fennell must have used it. And who knows what was going on while she was dreaming up the story.
reviews.author: Bill Goodykoontz

reviews.text: Fennell gives us such great dialogue in “Saltburn,” but not an inspired story. Though that’s certainly fun to watch, particularly among a large theatrical audience that’s game for it, it leaves a lot to be desired.
reviews.author: Candice Frederick

reviews.text: Although Saltburn is let down by a third act that is interesting but contradicts everything that came before it, you have to stand up and salute a film that's so eager to have "weird" and "horny" be its key descriptors.
reviews.author: Audrey Fox

reviews.text: [Keoghan has] his own charisma, which he plays [close to Alec] Guinness. A little bit of rough. Then an hour or so in, you get the shape of what’s happening.
reviews.author: Ray Pride

reviews.text: If the film's aggressive appetite for transgression eventually begins to feel like affectation, well, there is an awful lot of good unclean fun to be had on the way.
reviews.author: Robert Horton

reviews.text: There’s no rhythm to the film, no sense of buildup and payoff. There are occasional perverse pleasures... but there is little satisfaction to be found in the picture’s messily uninhibited climax.
reviews.author: Wendy Ide

reviews.text: Fennell has led us down the corridors of Salburn’s maze but with all the twists and turns it seems everyone has gotten lost along the way
reviews.author: Emily Maskell

reviews.text: The most sublime and rewarding subversion of the mythical straight boy unicorn trope. Emerald Fennel delivers a film whose opulence borders on fantasy and whose excess borders on the absurd in all the most rewarding ways.
reviews.author: Alachia Queen

reviews.text: Saltburn salaciously romps through obvious psychological machinations, orgiastic revelry, and ruthless elitist culling. Efforts to shock, disgust, and titillate devolve into banality. There are few surprises in a film that broadcasts its intentions.
reviews.author: Julian Roman

reviews.text: Even though Saltburn pushes the limits of what we’ve seen depicted onscreen, the story has plenty of superior, more beguiling antecedents.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: Saltburn ends up a titillation of flesh and nothing more.
reviews.author: Dustin Chang

reviews.text: The ingenuity of the story’s twists and turns ultimately left me feeling cheated, because of the cagy way that plot points are dispensed.
reviews.author: Richard Brody

reviews.text: As a class satire, it reaches no conclusions. But it’s filled to the brim with darkly funny, bile-slicked revulsion. For its director, who hails from the same upper classes she targets, it’s an act of self-excavation.
reviews.author: Clarisse Loughrey

reviews.text: A two-hour movie with an entertaining hour and a half followed by a formulaic climax and a reveal that stretches the probability so thin it snaps.
reviews.author: Michael J. Casey

reviews.text: Consistently perverse and often visually startling, it’s nevertheless weirdly unsatisfying. But it’s worth it to see Richard E. Grant, 66, and Rosamund Pike, highly entertaining as Elordi’s dotty parents.
reviews.author: Glenn Kenny

reviews.text: [Promising Young Woman] combined entertainment value with a serious point in a very well-tuned way. This follow-up tries to keep the shock value high, and ladles on the comedy of extremes, but it all seems more for effect than illumination.
reviews.author: James Saynor

reviews.text: There is nothing old or dull about this in-your-face black comedy.
reviews.author: Grant Rollings

reviews.text: Emerald Fennel’s new film is a prickly class satire wrapped in an opulent tale of desire.
reviews.author: Lyvie Scott

reviews.text: This is a coldblooded heart-clencher about inequality.
reviews.author: Amy Nicholson

reviews.text: Saltburn seems inspired by Brideshead Revisited and The Talented Mr. Ripley, with a touch of Absolutely Fabulous. Although not as great as these inspirations, Saltburn has memorable performances and eye-catching scenes. The ending has a major plot hole.
reviews.author: Carla Hay

reviews.text: It's tough and sinewy and the sex is so closely interwoven with the urge to dominate and control that you feel by the end of it the entrails of the British class system have been laid bare.
reviews.author: Sandra Hall

reviews.text: [Writer/director Emerald Fennell] dares you not to clutch your pearls.
reviews.author: Kent Turner

reviews.text: So much high-class satire has been on our screens lately like TV’s “Succession” and films such as “Parasite” and “Triangle of Sadness,” yet Fennell’s jokes are the laugh-out-loud sort that come as a surprise every time.
reviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski

reviews.text: “Saltburn” succeeds in slashing our expectations about how people are supposed to behave in polite society.
reviews.author: Christy Lemire

reviews.text: An invigoratingly nasty and hilarious piece of work... Saltburn doesn’t just want to let us vicariously live the fantasy life. It wants to hollow the fantasy life out and wear its skin and do a horny dance on its grave.
reviews.author: Jason Adams

reviews.text: The British class system has been well documented over the years in a multitude of ways. Fennell’s illustration is more captivating than most.
reviews.author: Jeanne Kaplan

reviews.text: Keoghan’s performance is one of great courage and daring.
reviews.author: David Kaplan

reviews.text: It’s little wonder Oliver is enchanted by her. But the movie around her is too smug by half. Elsbeth deserves her own picture...
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: Saltburn, despite all its lavish qualities and fun throwbacks, is an overstuffed and at times dated dive into society’s obsession with how the other half lives.
reviews.author: Jenny Nulf

reviews.text: The cast, which includes Richard E Grant, a cameoing Carey Mulligan and a scene-stealing Rosamund Pike as Felix's mother, are excellent. Though the film proves a little too invested in its own shocking reveals, you won't forget them in a hurry.
reviews.author: Matt Glasby

reviews.text: May be an accurate depiction of how chaotic stalkers can be. Unfortunately, the film can scare off viewers like an actual stalker.
reviews.author: Fred Topel

reviews.text: The frustration is that much works here. Fennell sets off in the right direction. A strong cast helps her on her way. But conviction falters long before the tables are kicked over.
reviews.author: Donald Clarke

reviews.text: Sex, drugs and a soundtrack filled with mid-noughties indie bangers (MGMT, The Killers and more) fuel a sunny vacation packed with illicit fun
reviews.author: Alex Flood

reviews.text: Its problem is that it’s superficially smart and deeply stupid. It’s clever and amusing in 20 different ways, but when it really matters, it descends into ridiculousness.
reviews.author: Mick LaSalle

reviews.text: Unspools as a satisfying, slow-burn mystery with dashes of pitch dark humour, though it is pitted with some annoying story flubs.
reviews.author: Jim Schembri

reviews.text: While there are traces of underlying poison laced throughout these sumptuous visuals, Saltburn is more invested in its own aesthetics than it is in its ostensible class satire.
reviews.author: Abby Monteil

reviews.text: I was often watching though my fingers. It is fearless -- and intoxicatingly so.
reviews.author: Deborah Ross

reviews.text: Fun to watch, difficult to love, Emerald Fennell’s film is lively, ambitious, a dizzying treat for its opening hour. The second hour, however, is another story entirely, and Saltburn eventually collapses in on itself.
reviews.author: Chris Wasser

reviews.text: An intoxicating, intense and exhilarating ride through the upper echelons of British high society, underpinned by bravura performances from the delightfully well-chosen cast.
reviews.author: Sarah McIntyre

reviews.text: “Saltburn” is the sort of embarrassment you’ll put up with for 75 minutes. But not for 127.
reviews.author: Wesley Morris

reviews.text: This seemingly provocative exploration slowly transitions into a silly and depraved episode of any random crime fiction podcast.
reviews.author: Joseph Robinson

reviews.text: There's deceptively little happening beneath the surface, but as a comedy-horror of jaw-droppingly poor behaviour in a gorgeous setting, it's a lot of filthy-minded fun.
reviews.author: Graeme Tuckett

reviews.text: The film keeps bellowing in your ear. Around now you may again ask yourself that original question: what is this movie meant to be?
reviews.author: Danny Leigh

reviews.text: A delicious cuckoo-in-the-nest story.
reviews.author: Gary M. Kramer

reviews.text: Saltburn’s seductive imagery outweighs its obvious attempts at provocation. And while it does end up making being rich look pretty sweet, that’s not exactly a revelation worth hanging a whole movie on.
reviews.author: Alison Willmore

reviews.text: Richly entertaining and extravagantly devious, Saltburn is a tale of twisted depravity that fits right in alongside films such as The Talented Mr. Ripley, The Rules of Attraction, and Cruel Intentions.
reviews.author: Kat Hughes

reviews.text: A film best left untainted so viewers can truly experience the descent into blackly comedic tragedy for themselves, Saltburn may flirt with narrative familiarity, but it plays out in a manner that many will be unprepared for.
reviews.author: Peter Gray

reviews.text: Refreshing, naughty, shocking, and unforgettable, it's a deliciously twisted tale of obsession and desire that is just as alluring as it is sickening.
reviews.author: Doug Jamieson

reviews.text: Sinister and beautifully uncomfortable with bonkers twists and a fearless turn from Barry Keoghan, but brought down by a narrative covering recent familiar social class themes without adding much to the discussion
reviews.author: Robert Kojder

reviews.text: This is a slow burn thriller that will shock and even disgust at time but it is a modern day masterpiece and I have to say I absolutely loved this film.
reviews.author: David Griffiths

reviews.text: A week after seeing the film, lines – particularly from Rosamund Pike – are still bouncing around in my head, prompting a smile and an urge to return to it.
reviews.author: Scott Nye

reviews.text: Saltburn’s a mess—a hot mess, at that!—but it’s also never boring.
reviews.author: Pat Mullen

reviews.text: Saltburn joins a myriad of recent movies about the super-rich (The Menu and Triangle of Sadness to name a few) and, like those films, don't expect to find yourself rooting for anyone.
reviews.author: Danny Brogan

reviews.text: Fennell creates a neo-gothic bonfire—a scion to Gatsby, Ripley, Six Degrees—that indicts the excesses & peculiarities of old-money wealth while exposing its underbelly. In the end, it isn’t about slaying the dragon as much as dissecting its anatomy.
reviews.author: Sherin Nicole

reviews.text: It feels as though Saltburn pulls you in two directions, asking you to keep an eye on this outsider and feeling some contempt for these people with a massive amount of fortune.
reviews.author: Murjani Rawls

reviews.text: The movie steps in and out of the don’t-go-there zone with admirable abandon.
reviews.author: Leigh Paatsch

reviews.text: Fennell’s feature all-too-frequently fumbles, misunderstanding character construction and misjudging the audience’s intellect in sussing out her anti-hero’s deviant actions.
reviews.author: Courtney Howard

reviews.text: A lesser 'Talented Mr. Ripley,' but still a ripping yarn
reviews.author: Jordan Hoffman

reviews.text: Fennell’s second feature is both evocative and provocative, with lashings of style but questionable substance. It doesn’t stick the landing, but the ride right before the nosedive is a properly enjoyable one.
reviews.author: Sophie Butcher

reviews.text: As a trashy, sexy thriller, Saltburn is superb, but if you’re after something a little more substantial, this isn’t it.
reviews.author: Maria Lattila

reviews.text: With a story that feels like the work of Patricia Highsmith filtered through a millennial lens, there’s a lot to appreciate about this film that extends beyond just the elaborate country house where these characters reside.
reviews.author: Aaron Neuwirth

reviews.text: Gorgeous, lurid, shallow and frustrating.
reviews.author: Hannah Strong

reviews.text: Saltburn is visually spectacular, thematically ambitious and features some of the most visceral, jaw-dropping scenes in cinema this year. But it lacks a cohesive throughline.
reviews.author: Wenlei Ma

reviews.text: Fennell’s latest resembles a sugar high: invigorating in the moment but insubstantial once it wears off.
reviews.author: Clint Worthington

reviews.text: Never more than skin-deep and ultimately overstays its welcome but which comes alive when—especially in its latter half—it indulges in its most wildly deviant impulses.
reviews.author: Nick Schager

reviews.text: Fennell definitely adds a potent dose of (very, very) dark humour into Saltburn.
reviews.author: Cat Woods

reviews.text:
Nothing can prepare you for Saltburn

An unsettling twisted  puzzle box of darkness,obsession, kink, & desire. 

Emerald Fennell stuns again with a slow riveting tale that will have your jaw drop 

Keoghan delivers such a fearless performance
reviews.author: Zach Pope

reviews.text: It all comes together as a tantalizing feast for the senses, a maximalist epicurean delight, bound by an outstanding ensemble cast and penetrating themes.
reviews.author: Matt Oakes

reviews.text: Lavish, intoxicating, and audaciously provocative, Saltburn is a fearless work from Fennell. A wicked character study that delivers an uncompromising look at social class, eroticism, and youth. It’s an amusement park of sex, lies and seduction.
reviews.author: David Gonzalez

reviews.text: Depraved English drama about class-conflict.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: As a viewer, it’s like being at one of the exotic, rule-breaking parties that happen in Brideshead and in this modern reinvention.
reviews.author: Stephen Romei

reviews.text: “Your politeness is so grating,” Venetia tells Oliver. So, too, is Fennell’s faux-rebelliousness. In Saltburn, the director has fallen into the same trap as a first-year Oxbridge student -- thinking flair can distract from having very little to say.
reviews.author: Simran Hans

reviews.text: As the window between cinema and v.o.d release gets shorter and shorter, if you’re still yet to see this delicious chaos from Emerald Fennell – now’s your chance.
reviews.author: Charlotte Harrison

reviews.text: Be it sexuality, gender, class, age, or race, there’s scarcely a hot-button issue of identity that Emerald Fennell won’t invoke to amplify the stakes of an obvious metaphor.
reviews.author: Marshall Shaffer

reviews.text: The darkly funny Saltburn confirms Emerald Fennell is a bold, exciting filmmaker and Barry Keoghan is one of our best young actors. But its determination to push the envelope makes it a hard movie to love.
reviews.author: Michael Balderston

reviews.text: A delicious exploration of class conflict and psychosexual jealousy
reviews.author: Stephen Silver

reviews.text: Mischievous in the best of ways.
reviews.author: Dan Scully

reviews.text: What remains is the sensation of loss one experiences when all that has come before has led to naught. It’s salt in our wounds, and burns mightily.
reviews.author: Christopher Llewellyn Reed

reviews.text: While Saltburn may not be as bracingly original as Fennell’s debut, it is wicked fun.
reviews.author: Stephen A. Russell

reviews.text: Anchored by a strong, eerie performance by Barry Keoghan, Saltburn is wickedly twisted, alluring, and darkly satirical, though it’s lacking some bite.
reviews.author: Mae Abdulbaki

reviews.text: A gorgeous misfire, a film that looks stunning but ultimately has nothing to say.
reviews.author: Brian Tallerico

reviews.text: Vicious swipes are delivered with backhanded relish by an excellent cast in stiff-upper-lip mode. Where the story goes is vivid and unnerving, simply because the storytelling is so full-on. We may have seen it before, but never quite like this.
reviews.author: Rich Cline

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell’s stylish sophomore feature Saltburn drips with tawdry intrigue and a myriad of bodily fluids as it slides down the dizzying spiral banisters of extravagant wealth and moral depravity.
reviews.author: Maggie Lovitt

reviews.text: Saltburn is imperfect, but like the titular estate it snags you in its grip and doesn’t let go.
reviews.author: Travis Hopson

reviews.text: It is pop art perversion. It is edgelord elegance. It is Grand Guignol that is likely to turn some away with the force of a wind tunnel, but is sure to find a loving home amongst the true freaks out there.
reviews.author: Cain Noble-Davies

reviews.text: Saltburn expertly dramatizes the intoxication of lust and the limits we all blow past while under its influence. Fennell’s live-wire pacing is perfectly complemented by the committed cast, particularly Barry Keoghan, Jacob Elordi and Rosamund Pike.
reviews.author: Christopher James

reviews.text: Saltburn is a sequined and sticky mess, every ensuing plot twist delivered like a bludgeon to the temple—with new developments echoing over viewers with a dizzying ferocity.
reviews.author: Anna McKibbin

reviews.text: At its funniest it's a proper hoot, and at its darkest, it's still strangely compelling.
reviews.author: Brian Viner

reviews.text: It’s easy to get lost in Saltburn’s sensational style, but its underwhelming storytelling and drab commentary break the illusion.
reviews.author: Jeff Nelson

reviews.text: An unreliable narrator, self-aware quips about Evelyn Waugh and shots cribbed from Last Year at Marienbad suggest nothing is quite what it seems – unless, that is, you’ve seen The Talented Mr Ripley and The Favourite.
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: Saltburn does seem a bit half-hearted. For that matter, it also lacks the focused anger of Promising Young Woman. Still, if you see it as a lurid pulp fantasy rather than a penetrating satire, then Saltburn is deliriously enjoyable.
reviews.author: Nicholas Barber

reviews.text: Like Emerald Fennell’s fabulous debut feature Promising Young Female, this is again driven by social critique, and a bold desire to shock, but it lacks the earlier film’s acuity and freshness; ultimately, it feels rather trite.
reviews.author: Demetrios Matheou

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell’s Saltburn is a wickedly subversive, exquisitely twisty character study that leaves no room for redemption and satisfying resolutions, and that’s the real genius of it.
reviews.author: Serena Seghedoni

reviews.text: ‘Saltburn’ is everything we assumed it would be but also somehow more than we ever could’ve dreamed. It defies expectations and refuses to settle for a simple indictment of the rich because that would be too easy.
reviews.author: Sharai Bohannon

reviews.text: Aside from a few pacing issues, Saltburn delivers an uncompromising vision from Emerald Fennell, an Oscar-winning writer director with a unique voice.
reviews.author: Martin Carr

reviews.text: Saltburn is a wildly entertaining multigenre extravaganza that features red-hot performances, especially from Barry Keoghan and Rosamund Pike. Its final act goes too far, but its commitment to its premise, comedy and production value make it a must-see.
reviews.author: Hamish Calvert

reviews.text: The film’s secret ingredient, though, is its sheer, nude-bungee-jumping-level fearlessness. British cinema hasn’t been this badly behaved since the days of Nic Roeg and Ken Russell, and was frankly in need of the shake-up.
reviews.author: Robbie Collin

reviews.text: If Saltburn’s knowing jabs at selfish high society feel pretty familiar... Pike’s preening and backbiting provides sheer scene-stealing pleasure.
reviews.author: Kate Stables

reviews.text: It’s like Bridgerton on amphetamines. Or Downton in a K-hole. And it’s appealing because, however fanciful and thematically absurd, there is truth here.
reviews.author: Kevin Maher

reviews.text: Saltburn doesn’t eat the rich so much as it licks them, slurps them, and then spits them back out.
reviews.author: Emma Kiely

reviews.text: Keoghan’s physicality and on-screen intensity allows the audience to see his perspective on an otherwise inaccessible world...a sensually disturbing yet utterly absorbing watch.
reviews.author: Katie Smith-Wong

reviews.text: The entire cast give it their very professional all, and what great stuff from Pike.
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: Saltburn is the work of a filmmaker working from a place of self-assured confidence. It feels like a glorious announcement of the kind of work we can expect from Fennell going forward. Bring it on.
reviews.author: Abby Olcese

reviews.text: It’s in service of the dizzying adventure of a story, undoubtedly wrestling with class and deception as much as desire and the plain silliness of youth. It’s all there, but one of the greatest pleasures of Saltburn is just being invited to the party.
reviews.author: Ella Kemp

reviews.text: Saltburn isn’t content with merely eating the rich. It wants to salivate on them like a fly readying its meal; it devours them slowly, savoring every tender morsel.
reviews.author: Britt Hayes

reviews.text: Saltburn is dynamite, bursting with lust, lies, and laughs — the kind edged with a dark snarl. If loving a movie this willfully seedy, boldly savage, smoking hot, and unnervingly sensational is wrong, then being right is boring.
reviews.author: Kristy Puchko

reviews.text: Fennell does a sly job of altering the interpersonal dynamics all throughout and not revealing her characters’ true natures until the very end, but she also overplays her hand in a third act that irreversibly reverses the clever-to-silly ratio.
reviews.author: Michael Nordine

reviews.text: "Saltburn" is a different kind of monster movie.
reviews.author: Jacob Hall

reviews.text: A dark and twisted thriller that isn't afraid to push boundaries. It gets weird, sexy, and unsettling, which all works for the story being told. Barry Keoghan delivers a career best performance.
reviews.author: Tessa Smith

reviews.text: Saltburn is a perverted fairytale of manic infatuation and greed dusted with toxic glitter and coated in splotchy fake tans stuffed into the world of contemporary British classism.
reviews.author: Jillian Chilingerian

reviews.text: Saltburn is stunning and hands-down Emerald Fennell’s best and most painstakingly precise work that doesn’t sacrifice emotion and intimacy for twisting pay-off.
reviews.author: Kate Sánchez

reviews.text: Emerald Fennell commands this artistically bold and masterfully crafted film, securing her place as a visionary filmmaker and auteur.
reviews.author: Ashley Menzel

reviews.text: Saltburn does not quite show the, eh, promise of the Promising Young Woman's director's obvious talent in that it tells a mostly predictable story but it is a highly entertaining and visually delightful picture nonetheless
reviews.author: J. Don Birnam

reviews.text: Its endless visual and literary layers will bring its ardent admirers back to it again and again, because it is a triumph of the cinema of excess, in all its orgiastic, unapologetic glory.
reviews.author: Maureen Lee Lenker

reviews.text: Fennell bravely holds up a mirror to the audience and says, "What if I didn't move the camera away and just let you watch your most depraved thoughts manifest onscreen?"
reviews.author: Sophia Ciminello

reviews.text: Saltburn is the most batshit crazy film you’ll see this year. It’s exquisitely shot, and Fennell directs the hell out of it. This is one of those films you won’t be able to stop thinking about for days after seeing it.
reviews.author: Scott Menzel

reviews.text: Barry is absolutely fearless in a role that requires a considerable amount of skill and nuance to pull off convincingly, and he does so to the point that it makes your skin crawl.
reviews.author: Matt Neglia

reviews.text: “Saltburn” works as a distinct and wildly entertaining probe into familiar waters of privilege, rather than the definite word on it, one that reinforces Fennell as a distinguished auteur of the big and the bold even on shaky grounds.
reviews.author: Tomris Laffly

reviews.text: You feel the influence of “The Talented Mr. Ripley” in Emerald Fennell’s screenplay (in more ways than one) and the twists and turns of “Dangerous Liaisons” aren’t far behind.
reviews.author: Gregory Ellwood

reviews.text: From start to finish, Saltburn is a wild and savage spellbinder. Transfixing and hypnotic, Emerald Fennell has crafted a provocative and diabolical masterpiece steeped in lies, deception, and a multitude of twists and turns.
reviews.author: Mark Johnson

reviews.text: A stylish but ultimately silly patchwork of borrowed ideas.
reviews.author: David Rooney

reviews.text: Fennell’s debut promised a fearless original voice and style. “Saltburn” certainly has attitude, but nothing new to say.
reviews.author: Peter Debruge

reviews.text: A spikily entertaining, narratively rackety ride led by a formidable Barry Keoghan in devil-may-care mode.
reviews.author: Fionnuala Halligan

reviews.text: A furiously candied pop confection whose most beautiful flourishes never seem to add up.
reviews.author: David Ehrlich

reviews.text: Saltburn proves an engaging sit for the majority of its run, and thus a stumble -- even a big one -- can mostly be forgiven. If anything, the film makes me curious to see what Fennell might do with another classic novel.
reviews.author: Richard Lawson

reviews.text: Saltburn is an audacious and exquisite display of Emerald Fennell and Barry Keoghan's powers.
reviews.author: Joey Magidson

reviews.text: [Emerald Fennell] reveals a strong hand behind the camera, even if the trajectory of the story feels rather overwrought and familiar. Nonetheless, the writing is alive and often amusing, giving the fine cast a lot to play with.
reviews.author: Todd McCarthy

synopsis: Academy Award winning filmmaker Emerald Fennell (Promising Young Woman) brings us a beautifully wicked tale of privilege and desire. Struggling to find his place at Oxford University, student Oliver Quick (Barry Keoghan) finds himself drawn into the world of the charming and aristocratic Felix Catton (Jacob Elordi), who invites him to Saltburn, his eccentric family's sprawling estate, for a summer never to be forgotten.
